oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Navigating The Leadership Labyrinth in Indonesian Higher Education: A Woman Confronting Dual Glass Barriers
oai_dc:dc.dc:creator: Respati, Yudit Ayu
Sawitri, Hunik Sri Runing
Sunaryo, Sinto
Hendarsjah, Hidajat
oai_dc:dc.dc:description:
We examined how a female rector navigates leadership barriers at an Islamic private university in Indonesia through the lens of the leadership labyrinth metaphor. The rector serves as the institution's highest executive leader. The metaphor conceptualizes leadership as a non-linear process shaped by multiple, intersecting barriers, making it particularly relevant for understanding women's leadership trajectories. A qualitative single-case study design was employed. Data were collected through in-depth semi-structured interviews with the female rector and seven supporting participants representing university leaders, faculty, and administrative staff, students, family, and leaders of the Islamic organization overseeing the university. Data were analyzed using the Gioia methodology to ensure methodological rigor and analytical transparency. Findings reveal, through systematic qualitative analysis, that the leadership trajectory is shaped by two interrelated barriers: the glass cliff and the glass ceiling. The glass cliff emerged through appointment during a period of organizational crisis, while the glass ceiling manifested in symbolic resistance and doctrinal religious interpretations. These barriers form a labyrinthine structure that requires continuous navigation. The study identifies six strategies for navigating this structure, reflecting rational agency in decision-making. By integrating role congruity theory and rational choice theory, we offer an empirically grounded conceptual illustration of the relationship between leadership barriers and individual navigation strategies, with implications for leadership development and advancement-focused policies in faith-based higher education.
Keywords: Women's Leadership, Labyrinth Metaphor, Barriers in Indonesian Higher Education, Role Congruity Theory, Rational Choice Theory
